identity.title: Embedded Systems Fundamentals
identity.tagline: The design habits that come with running code on small, resource-limited hardware instead of a full desktop computer.

simpleSummary: The particular design habits needed when running code on small, limited hardware like an Arduino — tiny memory, often no operating system at all, and direct control over the hardware itself.
keyIdea: Embedded systems run on hardware with tightly limited memory and processing power, often with no full operating system at all, requiring different programming habits than desktop software: careful memory use, direct hardware register access, and close attention to real-time constraints.
overview: Embedded programming differs from desktop or server software in a few fundamental ways. Memory is severely limited — kilobytes rather than gigabytes; an Arduino Uno, for instance, has just 2KB of SRAM to work with, compared to the gigabytes available on an ordinary computer. There is often no operating system at all: code runs directly on the bare hardware (sometimes called 'bare metal' programming), with the program itself entirely responsible for everything an OS would normally handle. Direct hardware access — writing to specific hardware registers to configure a timer's exact behavior, for example — is common, rather than calling a generic OS-provided API. And embedded systems very frequently control physical hardware in real time, tying this topic closely to real-time systems concepts.
howItWorks: These constraints shape real, practical programming habits. Memory management must be careful and deliberate: dynamic memory allocation that could fragment or exhaust a tiny, fixed memory pool over a device's long unattended lifetime is generally avoided in favor of fixed-size buffers and static allocation decided at compile time. A library or dependency's memory and processing footprint matters immensely on tiny hardware in a way it never would on a desktop computer, where an extra few megabytes is essentially free. Direct register manipulation offers a lower-level, faster, and more precise alternative to convenient library functions whenever exact timing or an otherwise-unsupported hardware feature demands it. Hobby platforms like Arduino intentionally hide much of this complexity behind convenient functions (digitalWrite, analogRead, and similar), making embedded programming approachable for beginners — while professional embedded work frequently requires dropping down to this lower, more direct level for the performance or hardware capabilities those convenient abstractions don't expose.
diagramCaption: A desktop computer runs an application on top of a full operating system with abundant memory; an embedded microcontroller typically runs its program directly on the bare hardware, with only kilobytes of memory to work with.
realWorldExamples: An Arduino Uno running a simple sensor-reading loop entirely without any operating system, directly on bare hardware.
A professional embedded engineer configuring a microcontroller's timer registers directly for microsecond-precise PWM generation that a generic library function couldn't achieve.
A battery-powered embedded sensor node written to fit entirely within a few kilobytes of RAM, deliberately avoiding any dynamic memory allocation over its months-long unattended deployment lifetime.
commonMisconceptions: "Embedded programming is basically the same as regular desktop programming, just on smaller hardware" — the resource constraints and lack of an OS create genuinely different habits and real failure modes (memory exhaustion, fragmentation) that desktop developers rarely have to think about at all.

"You always need to write low-level register code for embedded projects" — for many hobby and even professional purposes, higher-level libraries and frameworks are perfectly adequate; dropping to register-level code is only needed for specific performance or capability requirements those libraries don't cover.

"More powerful embedded boards make these constraints irrelevant" — even a relatively capable board like an STM32 or Teensy still has real, fixed resource limits that matter far more than on a desktop computer, just at a higher ceiling than an 8-bit Arduino.
